42878641.text: Purpose To evaluate the diagnostic performance of postcontrast liver attenuation measured with coronary CT angiography (CCTA) for opportunistic detection of hepatic steatosis and to assess the impact of tube potential variation on optimal attenuation thresholds and overall performance. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included adult patients who underwent CCTA with concomitant unenhanced coronary Agatston scoring (January to December 2025). Moderate-to-severe hepatic steatosis was defined as unenhanced liver attenuation less than 40 HU. Postcontrast liver attenuation was measured using standardized regions of interest. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis with Youden index-based threshold determination. Associations between hepatic steatosis, Agatston score categories, and Coronary Artery Disease Reporting and Data System (CAD-RADS) categorizations were evaluated using likelihood ratio χ2 tests. Results Among 300 included patients (mean age ± SD, 55.6 years ± 12.0; 170 males), moderate-to-severe steatosis was present in 109 patients (36.3%). Postcontrast liver attenuation demonstrated high diagnostic performance across all settings (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve: 0.88, 0.95, and 0.89 at 100, 120, and 140 kVp, respectively). Optimal thresholds decreased with increasing tube potential (54, 47, and 40 HU at 100, 120, and 140 kVp, respectively). Patients with steatosis had a lower frequency of coronary artery calcium scores of zero (43.7% vs 57.6%) and a higher frequency of coronary artery calcium scores of 101-300 (11.7% vs 4.9%; P = .042), whereas CAD-RADS distribution was similar (P = .12). Conclusion Postcontrast liver attenuation measured with CCTA demonstrated promising diagnostic performance for opportunistic identification of moderate-to-severe hepatic steatosis across different tube potential settings. Hepatic steatosis was associated with coronary calcium burden but not with CAD-RADS categorization.

42899941.text: Encephalitis is a medical emergency characterized by inflammation of the brain parenchyma due to an infective cause or an immune-mediated process. Autoimmune encephalitis (AE) is characterized by a misdirected immune attack against neuronal structures, resulting in an inflammatory response. Triggers for the development of antibodies are often paraneoplastic or parainfectious. AE may occur in children or adults with symptoms including subacute onset of altered mentation, cognitive issues, drug-resistant epilepsy, movement disorders, and/or autonomic dysfunction. Limbic encephalitis is a common imaging feature of many forms of AE; however, cortical, basal ganglia, diencephalon, brainstem, and cerebellar involvement have been described. This article provides an overview of the general imaging appearances of AE, with a detailed discussion of key patterns encountered with common causes of AE, as well as a review of the relevant differential diagnoses, thus serving as a practical reference for radiologists.

42911391.label: Purpose
42911391.text: To characterize proximal and distal colonic laterality and appendiceal-base location on CT in patients with situs inversus and situs ambiguus.

42911391.label: Methods
42911391.text: This retrospective multicenter study included 79 patients identified from abdominal CT reports at three tertiary hospitals between December 2003 and March 2025 (70 with situs inversus; 9 with situs ambiguus). A radiologist assessed thoracoabdominal organ arrangement, proximal and distal colonic laterality, combined proximal-distal colonic laterality pattern, and appendiceal-base location. The end of the cecum was used when the appendiceal base was not visible. Distributions of colonic laterality between the two situs types were compared using exact tests.

42911391.label: Results
42911391.text: In situs inversus, the proximal colon was left-sided in 66/70 patients (94.3%; 95% CI, 86.2-97.8), the distal colon was right-sided in 67/70 (95.7%; 95% CI, 88.1-98.5), and a left-proximal/right-distal combined colonic pattern occurred in 64/70 (91.4%; 95% CI, 82.5-96.0). The appendiceal base or cecal surrogate was in the left lower quadrant in 61/70 (87.1%; 95% CI, 77.3-93.1). In situs ambiguus, the proximal colon was midline-crossing in 7/9 patients (77.8%; 95% CI, 45.3-93.7), and the distal colon was left-sided in 6/9 (66.7%; 95% CI, 35.4-87.9). Locations of the appendiceal base or cecal surrogate were distributed across all abdominal regions. Distributions of segmental and combined colonic laterality differed between situs inversus and situs ambiguus (all exact p < .001).

42911391.label: Conclusion
42911391.text: Situs inversus usually shows mirror-image colonic laterality and a left-lower-quadrant appendiceal base, but exceptions occur. In this cohort, situs ambiguus showed greater variability. Colonic laterality and appendiceal-base location should be directly assessed on CT rather than inferred from situs classification alone.

42925841.label: Background
42925841.text: Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) is associated with tumor progression in gastric cancer (GC), but its added value for predicting lymph node metastasis (LNM) remains unclear.

42925841.label: Purpose
42925841.text: This study aimed to construct a DR-DLR model that incorporates CT-based features from both VAT and tumor, with the goal of predicting LNM in GC patients, while investigating its biological relevance.

42925841.label: Methods
42925841.text: 855 GC patients were retrospectively collected across three clinical centers, divided into a primary cohort, one internal test cohort, and two independent external validation cohorts. An Attention Residual Transformation Network (ARTNet) extracted imaging representations from CT images. Feature representations and clinical variables were integrated using a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to build the DR-DLR model. Model performance, generalizability, prognostic value, and biological relevance were evaluated using internal/external testing, radiologist comparison, survival analysis, and radiogenomics analysis.

42925841.label: Results
42925841.text: Incorporation of VAT-derived features improved predictive performance compared with tumor-only models. The DR-DLR model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.898 (95 % CI: 0.817-0.946), 0.834 (95 % CI: 0.743-0.897), and 0.848 (95 % CI: 0.775-0.901) in the internal and two external test cohorts, respectively. It outperformed junior and senior radiologists in LNM assessment. Overall survival was shorter in high-risk patients than in low-risk. Radiogenomics analysis revealed that the high-risk phenotype was associated with activation of immune-related pathways and increased infiltration of CD4 + T cells, plasma cells, dendritic cells, and mast cells.

42925841.label: Conclusion
42925841.text: The DR-DLR model improved LNM prediction, with its high-risk phenotype linked to immune-related molecular alterations, supporting its value for preoperative risk stratification.

42961641.label: Purpose
42961641.text: To evaluate the incremental prognostic value of visually assessable CT features beyond clinical stage (cStage) for disease-free survival (DFS) risk stratification in gastric cancer.

42961641.label: Methods
42961641.text: Patients undergoing curative gastrectomy were retrospectively included in development and external cohorts. Clinical and pathological stages were reconstructed according to the AJCC 8th edition and simplified to three tiers. Clinical Stage, CT Imaging, and Combined models were evaluated for discrimination, calibration, bootstrap-corrected performance, and external validation. Incremental prognostic value was assessed using changes in the C-index and time-dependent AUCs. A development-derived CT Imaging Score (CIS) cutoff was locked for exploratory risk refinement within preoperative cStage strata.

42961641.label: Results
42961641.text: Among 886 patients (development, n = 698; external, n = 188), cStage-pStage concordance was 51.0% and 61.2%, respectively (linear-weighted κ = 0.387 and 0.513). In the development cohort, adding CIS to cStage increased the C-index from 0.648 to 0.805 (ΔC-index = 0.160, P = 0.002) and the 1-, 3-, and 5-year AUCs by 0.159, 0.184, and 0.193, respectively (all P = 0.001). The optimism-corrected C-index was 0.797 for the Combined model. External C-indices were 0.676, 0.694, and 0.695 for the Clinical Stage, CT Imaging, and Combined models, respectively. In the development cohort, CIS-high status was associated with worse DFS within cStage II (HR = 8.66, 95% CI: 5.59-13.42) and cStage III (HR = 5.78, 95% CI: 3.74-8.92), with associations retained after adjustment for postoperative pStage.

42961641.label: Conclusion
42961641.text: Integrating visually assessable CT imaging features with conventional cStage improved DFS prognostic discrimination in the development cohort, while the derived CIS further refined risk stratification within preoperative cStage groups.

42965591.text: Despite advances in cross-sectional imaging, adrenal biopsy plays a role in a small subset of lesions that remain indeterminate after complete imaging work-up or in which tissue diagnosis would alter management. Anatomic constraints around the adrenal glands can make safe percutaneous access technically challenging. This technical report describes a transfemoral transcaval approach to biopsy of a right adrenal mass directly abutting the inferior vena cava (IVC) that was not safely accessible by conventional percutaneous routes. Additionally, a concise review of contemporary adrenal biopsy indications and access routes is performed. Adapted from transfemoral transcaval liver biopsy, the technique uses right common femoral venous access, positioning of a reshaped metal guide cannula within the IVC at the level of the lesion adjacent to the right renal vein, and deployment of a core biopsy needle across the caval wall under combined fluoroscopic and ultrasound guidance, with cone-beam CT confirmation of needle position and completion venography to exclude caval injury. Diagnostic tissue was obtained without periprocedural complication; histopathology demonstrated an unexpected pheochromocytoma, a finding discussed here in detail due to its implications for pre-procedure biochemical evaluation. This limited experience demonstrates technical feasibility in carefully selected patients. The safety and comparative effectiveness of the technique require evaluation in larger series.

42975641.text: Cystic echinococcosis (CE), caused by the metacestode of Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato, is a zoonosis that remains endemic across the Middle East, the Mediterranean basin, North Africa and South America, and the liver is the organ most frequently involved. Because serological assays are of limited sensitivity and specificity, imaging carries the diagnostic burden: ultrasonography (US) is the cornerstone for initial diagnosis, staging, treatment planning and longitudinal follow-up; computed tomography (CT) best defines anatomical location, vascular relationships, mural calcification and acute complications such as rupture and superinfection; and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) more faithfully reproduces US-defined staging morphology than CT and provides superior soft-tissue contrast for assessing biliary involvement and separating CE cysts from cystic neoplasms. The aim of this pictorial review is fourfold: to illustrate the US, CT and MRI appearance of each World Health Organization Informal Working Group on Echinococcosis (WHO-IWGE) stage of hepatic CE and to explain how stage assignment translates directly into a stage-specific treatment decision-anti-parasitic treatment, percutaneous treatment, surgery or watch-and-wait; to present, stage by stage, the hepatic lesions that mimic CE and the findings that discriminate them; to depict the wall signs of the CE cyst that become visible with high-frequency linear transducers, including the three-layered wall, adherent brood capsules and hydatid sand; and to review the imaging of complicated CE together with the expected post-treatment appearance, procedure-related complications and the imaging strategy for detecting recurrence.

42986491.label: Objective
42986491.text: This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of dynamic [18F]FDG PET/CT metabolic parameters and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), individually and in combination, in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) receiving neoadjuvant immunotherapy plus chemotherapy.

42986491.label: Methods
42986491.text: We retrospectively analyzed 168 NSCLC patients treated with neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy followed by surgery. Pre- and post-treatment PET metabolic parameters assessed by iPERCIST and peripheral blood NLR were collected. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with Cox regression were performed to identify predictors of disease-free survival (DFS).

42986491.label: Results
42986491.text: During a median follow-up of 25.2 months (95% CI, 21.0-29.3 months), 59 patients experienced recurrence. Post-treatment PET metabolic parameters, their changes, and post-treatment NLR were significantly associated with DFS. Among these parameters, ΔSUVmax and post-treatment NLR were identified as independent prognostic factors. Patients were stratified into three risk groups according to the combination of ΔSUVmax and post-treatment NLR, with significantly different DFS outcomes among groups (p = 0.001). Patients achieving iCMR/iPMR according to iPERCIST criteria showed longer DFS than those without favorable metabolic response (p = 0.005) .

42986491.label: Conclusions
42986491.text: Dynamic PET metabolic parameters, and post-treatment NLR hold significant prognostic value following neoadjuvant immunotherapy plus chemotherapy in NSCLC. A combined model integrating PET metabolic parameters and post-treatment NLR stratified patients into distinct risk groups, suggesting potential utility in postoperative risk assessment.

43037691.label: Purpose
43037691.text: Utilization of multiphase CT for gastrointestinal bleeding (CT-GIB) has experienced widespread growth in recent years, yet meaningful clinical outcomes associated with increased utilization remain uncertain. This study examines the overall positivity rate for CT-GIB, evaluates variables associated with a positive scan, and assesses the relationship between a positive CT-GIB and subsequent clinical interventions.

43037691.label: Materials and methods
43037691.text: IRB approved retrospective analysis of 1,040 consecutive patients undergoing CT-GIB (Jan. 2019-Mar. 2025). Demographic (age, gender), hemodynamic (heart rate, blood pressure, shock index), laboratory (hemoglobin, platelets, INR, PT/P TT, albumin, BUN, creatinine) and clinical (anticoagulant use, hypertension, malignancy, cirrhosis) parameters were extracted from the electronic medical record within the 48-h periprocedural window. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify variables independently associated with three outcomes: a positive multiphase CT-GIB scan, endovascular intervention within 48 h, and endoscopic intervention within 48 h.

43037691.label: Results
43037691.text: Imaging volume increased 1,044% over the 6.25-year period. Active bleeding was detected in 143/1,040 (13.8%) of CT-GIB. Fourteen patients died within 48 h and were excluded from intervention analysis. Of the remaining positive cohort, 31/141 (22.0%), reflecting the cohort of 141 patients who survived the initial 48-h periprocedural window (i.e., after exclusion of 2 CTGIB+ patients who died within 48 h), underwent acute interventions within 48 h. Angiography was performed alone in 21/141 (14.9%), endoscopic intervention alone in 8/141 (5.7%), and both interventions were performed in 2/141 (1.4%). Variables independently associated with a positive multiphase CT-GIB: age > 65 years (OR = 2.15, 95% CI 1.41-3.30), male sex (OR = 1.54, 95% CI 1.06-2.22), and a nadir systolic BP < 105 mmHg (OR = 3.12, 95% CI 1.47-6.63). A positive multiphase CT-GIB was strongly associated with endovascular intervention (OR = 42.83, 95% CI 14.56-126.01; p < 0.001), but not with endoscopic intervention (OR = 1.53, 95% CI 0.73-3.23; p = 0.261).

43037691.label: Conclusion
43037691.text: Multiphase CT-GIB volumes increased exponentially while positive yields remained low. This study demonstrates associations between CT-GIB findings and subsequent treatment pathways and lays the foundation for prospective studies aimed at determining whether interventional pathway-specific imaging selection can be applied without compromising clinical safety.

43049891.label: Purpose
43049891.text: Prostate MRI is shifting toward biparametric protocols that omit the gadolinium-based dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) sequence - a decision validated entirely on cancer detection. Whether these protocols preserve the ability to estimate tumor grade, the quantity that drives management, has rarely been tested. Using unsupervised MRI "habitats" as a transferable probe, we asked whether the diagnostic contribution of MRI dissociates between detecting and grading prostate cancer.

43049891.label: Methods
43049891.text: Unsupervised k-means habitats of within-patient-normalized T2 and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), plus semi-quantitative DCE maps where available, were defined on PROSTATEx (training), frozen, and transferred unchanged to Prostate-MRI-US-Biopsy (external; 614 MRI targets and 12,809 biopsy cores with per-core Gleason) and QIN-Repeatability (test-retest). Under patient-grouped nested cross-validation we compared habitat, whole-lesion and clinical models, benchmarked habitats against ADC, validated habitat-pathology concordance against these cores, and tested whether the contribution of MRI dissociated between detection and grading.

43049891.label: Results
43049891.text: Low-ADC habitats localized clinically significant cancer across the gland (odds ratio up to 3.05; two lowest-ADC habitats captured significant cancer at twice the random-sampling rate) - but did not exceed whole-lesion radiomics or the ADC value itself (area under the curve 0.69 versus 0.69, cross-validated in the external cohort; cores 0.58 versus 0.62). In 107 MRI-detected lesions, ADC no longer separated grade groups (p = 0.79), whereas DCE time-to-peak did, remaining associated with grade after adjustment for ADC, zone and volume (adjusted p = 0.006; likelihood-ratio p = 0.026), although out-of-sample prediction was weak (cross-validated κ 0.05).

43049891.label: Conclusion
43049891.text: Diffusion localized significant cancer, but mean ADC did not separate grade in detected lesions; perfusion timing was associated with grade, yet predicted it poorly and has not been externally validated. Whether omitting contrast forfeits clinically useful grading information therefore remains an open question, to be tested before contrast-free protocols are adopted where grade estimation matters.
